title: #10 When Introducing a New Routine, Lower the Content Demands
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton argues that the underrated benefit of classroom habits and routines is not the time they save but the attention they save. Once a routine is familiar, students can spend their finite attention on the content of a task rather than its structure. The move he makes follows directly: while a routine is still new, its structure itself consumes attention, so the content should be deliberately easy until the routine is automatic. He illustrates with two routines from his own maths teaching - the silent-think, rehearse, vote-on-cue procedure for diagnostic questions, and the Venn diagram task - introducing each with simple content before raising the difficulty. The principle is an application of limited working memory to task design, compressed into his line that if the question is tough and the routine is new, nothing is getting learned.
points: Barton reframes routines as an attention-saving device, not just a time-saving one, freeing students' limited attention for subject content.
The practical rule is sequencing: pair a new structure with easy content, and raise content demands only once the structure is familiar.
His diagnostic-question routine (think in silence, rehearse the explanation, vote only when asked) is first practised on deliberately simple questions.
The Venn diagram example shows the same logic across task types - the first run uses basic shape sorting so the structure, not the maths, carries the novelty.
quotes: Habits and routines are one of the foundations of an effective learning environment. Their obvious benefit is the time they save - if students and teachers know what they are doing because they have done it before, they can just crack on and do it.

But habits and routines have another benefit - they save attention. If students (and teachers) know what is expected, they can dedicate less of their finite attention to the structure of tasks and activities, and more to the content of those tasks and activities, hence learning more in the process.
But when establishing habits and routines, those structures are not familiar. Hence, it is a good idea to lower their content demands initially.

But to get students to that stage, I first need to practice with relatively simple diagnostic questions - therefore allowing my students to dedicate more of their limited attention to the routines I want in place for answering the question. If the question is tough and the routine is new, nothing is getting learned.

But if the Venn Diagram structure itself is unfamiliar, then that is where students' attention will focus on. Hence, the first time I do a Venn Diagram task with my class, I keep the subject content simple - usually basic object shorting. That allows my students to get to the point where the structure of the task is familiar enough that I can raise the content demands.
